passages.t: The messenger, and the refiner's fire
passages.happening:
God answers the question where is the God of justice. ‘Behold, I will send My messenger, who will prepare the way before Me. Then the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to His temple’ (verse 1). He is the Messenger of the covenant, and he is coming.

‘But who can endure the day of His coming? And who can stand when He appears? For He will be like a refiner’s fire, like a launderer’s soap’ (verse 2). He will sit as a refiner of silver and purify the sons of Levi, and then their offerings will please the LORD again (verses 3-4). Then God will come near for judgment, against sorcerers, adulterers and perjurers, and against those who cheat workers of their wages, oppress the widow and the fatherless, and deny justice to the foreigner (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The people wanted God's justice. God says it is coming, but it will begin with them. The pictures come from two trades. A refiner melted silver in a furnace and skimmed off the impurities until the metal was pure. A launderer cleaned and whitened cloth with strong soap. Both purify, and both are harsh.

The refining starts with the priests, the sons of Levi, whose failures filled chapters 1 and 2. Then it reaches the whole community. The list in verse 5 shows that God's justice is not only about worship. It is about wages, widows, orphans and foreigners. Nehemiah confronted the same abuses when he made the nobles give back the fields and interest they had taken.

Verse 1 plays on the word messenger, the prophet's own name: first a messenger prepares the way, then the Messenger of the covenant comes.
passages.later: Mark opens his Gospel with this verse joined to Isaiah 40:3: ‘Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You, who will prepare Your way’ (Mark 1:2). Jesus said of John the Baptist, ‘This is the one about whom it is written’ (Matthew 11:10), and quoted it.
passages.hard:
Who is the messenger, and who is the Lord who comes to his temple?

In Malachi, the messenger prepares the way before the LORD himself, and then the Lord whom the people seek comes to his own temple. The New Testament identifies the messenger as John the Baptist (Matthew 11:10; Mark 1:2), and in the Gospels he prepares the way for Jesus. The implication, which the New Testament draws without stopping to argue it, is that in Jesus the LORD has come to his temple.

Christians differ on whether the Messenger of the covenant is the same figure as the Lord who comes or a different one, though most have understood both phrases to point to Christ. Jewish readers have understood the passage of God's own coming, and of the herald who will go before it.
passages.asks: The people wanted God's justice, and God said it would begin with them. Ask what it would mean to want his justice and also to fear it. And ask what in you needs the refiner's fire.

passages.happening:
‘Because I, the LORD, do not change, you descendants of Jacob have not been destroyed’ (verse 6). From the days of their fathers they have turned away. ‘Return to Me, and I will return to you’ (verse 7). They ask how. ‘Will a man rob God?’ (verse 8). They ask how they rob him. ‘In tithes and offerings’ (verse 8).

‘Bring the full tithe into the storehouse, so that there may be food in My house. Test Me in this,’ says the LORD of Hosts (verse 10), and see if he will not open the windows of heaven and ‘pour out for you blessing without measure’ (verse 10). He will stop the devourer from destroying the crops, and the vines will bear, and the nations will call them a land of delight (verses 11-12).
passages.hearers:
The law set apart a tenth of Israel's produce to support the Levites, who had no land of their own, and the Levites gave a tenth of that to the priests. Every third year the tithe also fed the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow. The storehouse was a set of rooms in the temple where these gifts were kept. Holding back the tithe starved the temple's service and the poor it helped feed.

Judah was struggling. Crops were threatened by drought and by the devourer, probably locusts, Persian taxes were heavy, and many people were in debt. In such times it was tempting to hold back. Nehemiah found that the Levites had not been given their portions and had gone back to their own fields.

The people's reply, ‘How can we return?’ (verse 7), shows that they do not think they have gone anywhere.
passages.later: Nehemiah restored the practice, and ‘all Judah brought a tenth of the grain, new wine, and oil into the storerooms’ (Nehemiah 13:12). The law of the tithe is in Numbers 18:21-28 and Deuteronomy 14:22-29.
passages.hard:
Does verse 10 promise financial reward to Christians who tithe?

Verse 10 is sometimes used to promise that those who give a tenth will be rewarded with wealth. The passage speaks to the covenant community of Judah under the law of Moses, whose tithes supported the Levites and the poor through the temple storehouse, and whose covenant promised good harvests on the land for obedience. God's challenge to test him is a call to trust him in a time of scarcity, and the good he names is rain and harvest for a farming people.

Christians differ on how tithing applies today. Some hold that the tenth remains a standard for believers, noting that it came before the law, with Abraham and Jacob, and that Jesus affirmed it in passing (Matthew 23:23). Others hold that the New Testament replaces a fixed share with generous, cheerful, proportionate giving (2 Corinthians 8 and 9). Both agree that withholding from God shows a lack of trust, and that God is faithful to provide. Neither reading supports the teaching that giving is a technique for getting rich.
passages.asks: God's call is first to return, and only then to give. Ask what your giving shows about whom you trust. And ask what returning to God would look like before anything else changes.

passages.happening:
‘Your words against Me have been harsh,’ says the LORD (verse 13). The people have said, ‘It is futile to serve God’ (verse 14). What have they gained by keeping his requirements? Now they call the arrogant happy, because evildoers prosper and test God and escape (verse 15).

‘At that time those who feared the LORD spoke with one another, and the LORD listened and heard them’ (verse 16). A scroll of remembrance was written before him about those who feared the LORD and honored his name. ‘They will be Mine,’ says the LORD of Hosts, ‘on the day when I prepare My treasured possession’ (verse 17). He will spare them as a father spares a son who serves him. Then they will see again the difference between the righteous and the wicked, between those who serve God and those who do not (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
This is the sixth argument, and it runs on into chapter 4. The complaint of verse 14 is the honest voice of people who kept the rules and saw nothing come of it, while the arrogant did well.

Verse 16 does something rare in the prophets. It stops quoting God and tells what people did: the faithful talked with one another, and God listened. Royal courts kept written records of loyal service, and in Esther the Persian king has his book of records read and finds a deed that has gone unrewarded. God, too, keeps a record, and nothing done in faith is forgotten.

Treasured possession is a word for a king's own treasure, the word God used of Israel at Sinai.
passages.later: At Sinai God said, ‘you will be My treasured possession out of all the nations’ (Exodus 19:5). Moses told Israel that God had chosen them ‘to be a people for His prized possession’ (Deuteronomy 7:6).
passages.asks: The faithful talked together when others said serving God was futile. Ask who you talk with when faith is hard. And ask whom you could seek out this week who might be close to giving up.
